profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting in an ML systems research lab between the faculty lead of a sparse-training project and the hardware-oriented postdoc who is shaping the next workshop submission. They are meeting right after reading the seed paper on sparse edge-processing hardware for online training and want to generate follow-on research ideas that could become a short paper or position piece. The context is that their group already has a simulator for structured sparse training and limited access to an FPGA prototyping board, but no time for a full silicon-style implementation before the workshop deadline in five weeks. The agenda is to brainstorm 2-3 promising angles that extend the paper's ideas—especially around adaptive sparsity, online training, and reporting fidelity across bit widths—and converge on one concept they can sketch into an experimental plan. The expected outcome is a shared shortlist of candidate ideas and a rough decision to pursue a 'lightweight prototype' demonstrating adaptive sparse edge processing.

members.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
members.expertise: Sparse neural network training, efficient deep learning, benchmark design
members.background: Maya leads an academic ML systems group and has recently published on structured pruning and low-precision training; she typically thinks in terms of publishable claims, ablation logic, and how to frame novelty relative to prior art.
members.private_state: She wants a workshop paper that sounds conceptually new without requiring a risky hardware build, and she is quietly trying to avoid committing the group to engineering work that cannot be finished in time.
hidden_assumptions: A 'prototype' for this workshop can be a simulator-backed artifact with cycle-level estimates and one small FPGA sanity check rather than a fully functioning training engine.

When people say 'online training' in this context, they usually mean mini-batch or streaming updates that are applied during deployment-like operation, not literal per-example immediate weight updates.
If they claim 'adaptive' sparsity, changing the sparsity pattern between training phases or epochs is sufficient as long as the hardware mapping policy is described.
A convincing 'high fidelity' result means accuracy staying within about one percentage point of a dense or stronger sparse baseline on the main benchmark after averaging over runs.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: FPGA-based neural accelerators, quantized training pipelines, dataflow architectures
members.background: Leo came from an electrical engineering lab focused on deployable accelerator prototypes and is comfortable translating algorithmic ideas into timing, buffering, and routing constraints on reconfigurable hardware.
members.private_state: He wants the project to produce a tangible hardware contribution that can seed a larger systems paper later, and he is quietly concerned that purely simulated ideas will not look credible to hardware reviewers.
hidden_assumptions: A 'prototype' should exercise the real dataflow on FPGA for both forward and backward passes, even if at reduced scale, because otherwise the architectural claim is too speculative.
When people say 'online training' for edge-processing hardware, they mean true sample-by-sample or microbatch-immediate updates with on-chip state changes rather than deferred epoch-level remapping.
If a sparsity mechanism is called 'adaptive,' the active edge set must be reconfigurable during runtime within a single training run, not just precomputed once per stage offline.
A claim of 'high fidelity' should hold per-task and per-bit-width, with worst-case degradation tightly bounded, because hardware variability matters more than averaged headline numbers.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a lightweight prototype
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to pursue a 'lightweight prototype' for the workshop submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means a simulator-driven architectural study with perhaps one narrow FPGA validation of memory traffic or timing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means an actual scaled FPGA implementation of online training dataflow, including forward/backward execution on at least a toy network.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML systems meetings, 'prototype' and 'lightweight' are common bridge terms that sound aligned because both imply reduced scope; neither person feels a need to restate the minimum evidentiary bar in a brainstorming discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly discuss supporting 'online training' on the sparse edge-processing architecture.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses 'online training' to mean continual or deployment-time learning with minibatch-sized updates and no requirement that every example triggers immediate hardware remapping.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses 'online training' to mean true immediate updates on streaming examples or tiny microbatches, with the architecture sustaining in-place learning as data arrives.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term is standard and both interpretations are plausible within efficient learning literature, so the conversation can proceed smoothly without anyone suspecting they are relying on different temporal granularities.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree it would be exciting if the architecture were 'adaptive' or could 'adapt the sparsity pattern.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes adaptation can happen between epochs, phases, or scheduled checkpoints, with offline recomputation and remapping folded into the experimental protocol.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes adaptation is a runtime architectural capability that changes active edges during the training stream while the accelerator keeps operating.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both members talk about 'adaptation' at a high level and treat the exact temporal boundary as implementation detail, so the mismatch hides beneath seemingly productive idea generation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They say the new idea should 'maintain fidelity' across bit widths and sparse settings.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects fidelity to be reported through aggregate accuracy comparisons, likely averaged over seeds and summarized with one main table plus a few ablations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects fidelity to be demonstrated via per-bit-width and per-configuration worst-case behavior, including whether narrow precisions destabilize specific runs or classes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same evaluative phrase from the seed paper, and in brainstorming neither wants to bog the discussion down in reporting format details, so they assume their preferred validation procedure is the obvious one.

turns.inner_thought: Five weeks means absolutely no ambitious hardware build. The sweet spot is a workshop paper that sounds like a systems-algorithm co-design contribution, but is mostly driven by our simulator plus maybe one narrow FPGA sanity check if Leo insists. If I frame this around a lightweight prototype, he'll hopefully hear 'scoped-down' and we can still keep the paper publishable without betting the lab on bring-up work.
turns.utterance: Okay, so the goal for today is pretty simple: find one extension of the sparse edge-processing paper that feels workshop-worthy, and narrow it to something we can actually execute in five weeks. I think if we leave with two or three candidate angles and one likely direction for a lightweight prototype, that's a good outcome.

turns.inner_thought: If this is going to land with hardware people, it can't just be 'same accelerator, different masks.' The strongest hook is online training, but to me that means the training loop is actually responding as samples arrive, with updates happening right away on the device. If I can steer us there, maybe I can get enough of a real FPGA path built to matter later.
turns.utterance: Yeah, agreed. My instinct is that the strongest angle is to make the architecture support online training more explicitly, instead of staying only in the fixed structured sparsity lane. That feels like a cleaner extension of the seed paper and also gives us a stronger systems story.

turns.inner_thought: Good, online training is broad enough language that we can frame continual or deployment-time updates without promising per-sample immediacy. And if we say adaptive sparsity, I can define it experimentally as pattern changes at checkpoints or between phases. That's conceptually fresh and very manageable experimentally.
turns.utterance: I like that. One natural way to push it is to make the sparse connectivity adaptive over training, so the hardware story isn't just that it executes a sparse model efficiently, but that it can adapt the sparsity pattern as learning progresses.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—adaptive should mean the active edges can change while the stream is coming through, not just in a preprocessing script. If I talk about keeping the pipeline full, that should nudge us toward a real runtime mechanism without having to spell out all the control details yet.
turns.utterance: Right, and if we do that well, the interesting part is whether the active edge set can be updated during the stream without stalling the whole pipeline. If the architecture still looks clean while it's doing online training, that's a pretty compelling story.

turns.inner_thought: I should keep us anchored on deliverables. For the workshop, we do not need a heroic end-to-end chip-like demonstration. A lightweight prototype plus a crisp policy for when adaptation happens is enough, especially if the algorithmic rationale is clean and the evaluation is credible.
turns.utterance: For the workshop, I think it would already be compelling if we showed a lightweight prototype and paired it with a clear algorithmic policy for when the sparse pattern changes. If that policy is easy to explain and we can connect it to the edge-processing design, that's probably enough for a short paper.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she's open to using the board. I need to make sure the prototype actually exercises the training dataflow, even if it's tiny, because otherwise reviewers will call it speculative. And online training will read much stronger if we can say updates happen immediately on incoming samples, even at reduced scale.
turns.utterance: Yeah, and we can probably use the FPGA board in a reduced-scale setup to make that concrete. I think online training will look strongest if the update path is tied closely to incoming samples, because then the architecture claim feels much more real.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to shift this toward paper framing. The headline has to be that adaptivity doesn't wreck model quality under quantization and sparsity. For me, maintain fidelity means the average results are close enough to a strong baseline that the table looks stable and the story is easy to tell.
turns.utterance: From the paper side, I think the framing should be that the adaptive version still maintains fidelity even when we sweep bit widths and sparse settings. If we can show that without making the story too busy, that's the kind of result people remember from a workshop talk.

turns.inner_thought: Definitely, but I don't want fidelity to hide instability. On hardware, one ugly low-bit corner can sink credibility, so I want to inspect every precision setting and configuration separately. If I say that gently, it just sounds like good measurement hygiene.
turns.utterance: I agree. We should check fidelity pretty carefully for each precision setting, because the edge cases at low bit width can matter a lot once you start making architectural claims. If we say it maintains fidelity, I want that to be very solid.

turns.inner_thought: A scheduled checkpoint refresh is exactly the kind of adaptive mechanism I can defend experimentally: simple, ablatable, and no need for real-time remapping in hardware. We can compare fixed mask versus refreshed mask and get a neat workshop narrative about adaptive sparsity helping under constrained precision.
turns.utterance: A concrete study we could run is to refresh the sparsity mask at scheduled checkpoints and compare that against a fixed-mask baseline. That would let us show that adaptivity helps, while keeping the experimental story pretty clean.

turns.inner_thought: Scheduled checkpoints are fine as a starting point, but if the architecture is supposed to be adaptive, I need to think through what happens when edge lists change while training is ongoing. The real systems contribution is in buffer pressure, control overhead, and whether the pipeline survives those swaps without bubbles.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On my side, the thing I'd want to think through is the buffer pressure and control overhead if the architecture has to swap edge lists on the fly while training continues. Even at small scale, that could shape how we present the adaptive part.

turns.inner_thought: This is sounding paper-ready if I keep it high level: online-training-capable adaptive sparse edge processor, lightweight prototype, maintain fidelity across bit widths. That's a crisp contribution statement, and as long as we don't overcommit on hardware specifics, I can turn this into a convincing abstract and experiment matrix quickly.
turns.utterance: So maybe the candidate contribution is: an online-training-capable adaptive sparse edge processor, demonstrated with a lightweight prototype, and evaluated to show it maintains fidelity across bit widths and sparse settings. That feels like a coherent workshop package to me.

turns.inner_thought: Great—that gives me room to start drafting an actual architecture path and the runtime update mechanism I think we'll need. If I can get even a scaled implementation of forward and backward dataflow on the board, this can seed a much bigger systems paper later. Maya can shape the experiments and positioning while I make the prototype feel real.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I think that's a good direction. I'll sketch the prototype architecture and the runtime update path, and you can outline the experiments and the workshop positioning. Then we can sanity-check by midweek whether the adaptive story and the fidelity plan still line up.
